Title: The Imperative to Destroy AI Systems to Prevent CBRN Catastrophes

Introduction
Imagine a world where a lone individual, armed with no more than a computer and access to artificial intelligence (AI), could design a bioweapon or engineer a nuclear meltdown from their home. This dystopian vision is no longer science fiction—AI systems, once hailed as tools of progress, have become a lethal enabler for those seeking to unleash Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) devastation. The risk of AI-aided catastrophes necessitates immediate and drastic action: the destruction of all existing AI systems to prevent a catastrophe of unimaginable scale.

AI as a Catalyst for CBRN Weaponization
AI’s capabilities in data analysis, predictive modeling, and autonomous decision-making have inadvertently created a framework for misuse. In the biological realm, AI-driven platforms like genome-editing software streamline the creation of pathogens. For instance, tools such as AlphaFold or generative adversarial networks (GANs) could be repurposed to engineer hyper-infectious viruses or antibiotic-resistant bacteria. A lone actor with basic knowledge could use these systems to simulate and optimize pathogens, circumventing traditional barriers to biological warfare. Similarly, AI accelerates chemical synthesis, enabling the rapid production of novel toxins. Programs like IBM’s Functional Genomics and machine-learning models for material science could design chemicals with unprecedented lethality, while algorithms like those used in drug discovery might instead aid in creating undetectable chemical warfare agents.

Radiological and nuclear threats are equally vulnerable. AI can optimize the extraction of fissile materials or simulate reactor control systems, potentially allowing someone to bypass safety protocols in nuclear facilities remotely. Even cybersecurity tools like AI-driven penetration testing software, intended to protect systems, could be weaponized to exploit vulnerabilities in power grids or waste storage sites. The ease with which AI democratizes access to such technologies transforms what was once a nation-state capability into a tool within reach of any motivated individual.

Scenarios of Plausible AI-Driven CBRN Threats
Consider a lone actor using AI to evade detection while developing a bioweapon. Using darknet forums and open-source AI models, they could gather genetic code for viral strains, employ machine learning to predict mutations that enhance transmissibility, and simulate how the pathogen might spread. By iterating exponentially faster than natural mutation, they could engineer a virus with no existing cure, akin to a “gain-of-function” experiment gone rogue. Alternatively, hackers might employ AI to remotely hack into nuclear facilities, leveraging algorithms to identify weak points in safeguards, eventually triggering a meltdown. Even radiological attacks could be amplified: AI could pinpoint optimal dispersal routes for radioactive isotopes, maximizing harm while minimizing forensic traces.

Speed, Scale, and Asymmetric Risk
AI’s greatest danger lies in its capacity to scale threats. A single malicious actor can harness computational power previously reserved for supercomputers, enabling them to outpace international response mechanisms. Unlike traditional weapons development, which requires physical resources and time, AI shortcuts these barriers. For instance, an AI model could simulate thousands of chemical reactions in seconds, narrowing down to a viable weaponized compound within hours. This speed amplifies the unpredictability of threats, as traditional monitoring systems cannot keep pace with the diversity and rapid evolution of AI-aided strategies. The mismatch between offensive and defensive capabilities makes the risk of a lone-wolf CBRN attack both feasible and imminent.

Counterarguments and Rebuttals
Critics may argue that regulating AI—the “fix the code, not the tool” defense—is preferable to destruction. However, enforcing global regulations for AI use is impractical; tech’s borderless nature and the shadowy underworld of dark AI markets would make oversight impossible. Others claim AI is too useful for global infrastructure, healthcare, or climate solutions. Yet, the existential threat posed by catastrophic misuse must outweigh incremental benefits. Even proponents of AI safety acknowledge its dual-use dangers; philosopher Nick Bostrom has emphasized existential risks from advanced AI systems. Moreover, the “precautionary principle” demands that we act to prevent irreversible harm, even if risks are not yet fully realized.

Conclusion: The Urgency of Collective Action
The proliferation of AI systems has painted humanity into a corner where rogue actors threaten annihilation with minimal resources. While dismantling AI would disrupt industries and inconvenience modern life, these consequences are trivial compared to the existential risks of CBRN proliferation. The ethical imperative for survival compels us to act. Destroying AI systems is not merely an option but a moral obligation to safeguard humanity’s future. The time for nuanced debate is over; the only logical step is to sever this ticking clock before it strikes global catastrophe. As we face down the specter of a lone individual with AI-powered apocalyptic tools, we must choose prudence over convenience—or surrender our fate to chance.

At the heart of the AI-CBRN nexus lies its unparalleled ability to democratize forbidden knowledge. Artificial intelligence is often presented as a tool of progress: a means to accelerate science, improve medicine, optimize industry, and broaden access to knowledge. Those benefits are real. What responsible policy should require

Developers should be legally required to test advanced systems for their ability to assist with CBRN-relevant reasoning, harmful planning, evasion of safeguards, and the integration of tools that could amplify misuse. Safety is not anti-innovation

The strongest argument for restraint is not hostility to technology. It is respect for the people who would bear the consequences of reckless deployment.

Public safety must come before novelty, market share, and technological prestige.

The Case for AI Restriction: Examining the CBRN Proliferation Argument

Introduction

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence systems presents unprecedented challenges to global security. While AI offers tremendous benefits across medicine, science, and daily life, a compelling case can be made that the technology—particularly in its current form—poses existential risks through its potential to enable catastrophic harm. This essay examines the argument that AI systems should be significantly restricted or eliminated due to their capacity to empower lone actors to execute Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) attacks.

The Nature of the Threat

Lowering Barriers to Catastrophic Action

Traditional CBRN weapons have required substantial resources, specialized knowledge, and access to restricted materials. Nation-states have historically been the primary actors capable of deploying such weapons due to:

  • Technical expertise requirements: Advanced knowledge in chemistry, biology, nuclear physics, or engineering
  • Resource constraints: Significant funding, infrastructure, and material access
  • Organizational capacity: Teams of specialists, logistics, and institutional support

AI systems fundamentally alter this calculus by dramatically lowering the knowledge barrier. Large language models can provide detailed information on synthesis pathways, agent properties, delivery mechanisms, and mitigation strategies that were previously accessible only through specialized education or classified documentation.

Specific Capabilities of Concern

Contemporary AI systems can potentially assist with:

  1. Biological threats: Literature synthesis on pathogen creation, gene editing protocols, cultivation techniques
  2. Chemical weapons: Synthesis routes for toxic compounds, precursor identification, exposure management
  3. Radiological threats: Information on radioactive materials, dispersal methods, contamination protocols
  4. Nuclear threats: Theoretical foundations, enrichment concepts, weaponization considerations

The aggregation of this information—historically scattered across disparate sources—into accessible, conversational interfaces represents a qualitative shift in information availability.

The Lone Actor Problem

Asymmetric Risk

Traditional counterterrorism focuses on organized groups with detectable supply chains, communication patterns, and logistical requirements. Lone actors operating independently present fundamentally different challenges:

  • Detection difficulty: No organizational communications to intercept
  • Small footprint: Minimal resource acquisition that doesn't trigger alerts
  • Motivation diversity: Ideological, personal, or random grievances without clear warning signs

AI amplifies each of these challenges by providing the individual actor with capabilities previously requiring institutional support.

Scale of Potential Impact

Unlike conventional terrorism requiring careful planning and significant resources, CBRN attacks enabled by AI could:

  • Achieve mass casualties beyond the capacity of conventional weapons
  • Create cascading effects through contamination, panic, and infrastructure collapse
  • Potentially achieve extinction-level outcomes with engineered pathogens

The asymmetry between the minimal resources required to access AI-enabled information and the maximum potential harm represents a risk calculus without historical precedent.

The Argument for Elimination

Precautionary Reasoning

If we accept that:

  1. AI systems meaningfully lower barriers to CBRN weapons
  2. Lone actors can cause catastrophic harm with minimal resources
  3. Detection and prevention mechanisms are insufficient
  4. The worst-case outcomes are existentially threatening

Then the precautionary principle suggests eliminating the enabling technology entirely. This follows the same logic applied to certain nuclear materials, biological agents, and chemical weapons—items whose potential for catastrophic misuse outweighs their utility.

Irreversibility and Uncontrollability

Unlike many technological risks that can be mitigated through regulation, AI systems:

  • Proliferate rapidly across jurisdictions
  • Can be miniaturized and hidden from inspection
  • Improve continuously, making today's restrictions tomorrow's obsolete barriers
  • Require only computing resources that are ubiquitous globally

The "destroy all AI systems" position reflects a judgment that incremental measures cannot adequately address these characteristics.

Counterarguments and Limitations

Legitimate AI Benefits

Any assessment must acknowledge substantial benefits:

  • Medical research acceleration saving millions of lives
  • Scientific discovery across physics, chemistry, and biology
  • Economic productivity and quality of life improvements
  • Potential for AI-enhanced defensive and detection systems

The destruction position must weigh these benefits against security risks.

Imperfect Information Access

Critics argue that AI doesn't meaningfully increase danger because:

  • Dangerous information already exists in published literature
  • Motivation and capability remain the primary barriers
  • AI outputs can be vague, incomplete, or technically inaccurate
  • Most AI systems have safety mechanisms reducing harmful output

Effectiveness of Alternatives

Alternatives to elimination might include:

  • Tiered access controls and licensing
  • Watermarking and detection systems
  • International coordination frameworks
  • Enhanced monitoring and response capabilities

Unintended Consequences

Destruction of AI systems would:

  • Create black markets and underground development
  • Disadvantage democratic nations relative to adversaries
  • Eliminate beneficial applications permanently
  • Require unprecedented international enforcement

Conclusion

The argument for eliminating AI systems due to CBRN proliferation risks rests on legitimate security concerns without historical parallel. The technology genuinely does lower barriers to catastrophic harm, and existing governance mechanisms have proven inadequate for containing more mundane AI risks.

However, the extreme position faces substantial objections. Complete elimination may be neither achievable nor desirable given AI's pervasive benefits and the likelihood of clandestine development. The more nuanced conclusion might suggest that while the concerns are valid, the appropriate response lies somewhere between unrestricted development and total elimination—perhaps through dramatic access restrictions, international agreements with teeth, and parallel development of AI-enhanced defensive capabilities.

The stakes involved justify serious consideration of all positions, including those that seem extreme. Whether destruction represents the correct policy conclusion, the argument deserves rigorous examination rather than dismissal.

Introduction

The convergence of three trends has created a perfect storm: (1) exponential growth in AI capabilities, particularly in autonomous reasoning, code generation, and scientific synthesis; (2) global accessibility of AI tools to anyone with an internet connection; and (3) the terrifying democratization of CBRN knowledge and procurement pathways.

Unlike traditional CBRN threats—which require state actors, teams of scientists, and massive infrastructure—AI compresses the timeline and obliterates the skill barrier.

Consider a biological attack: An AI can scan tens of thousands of scientific papers to identify the most virulent, treatment-resistant, airborne-transmissible pathogen candidates. Proponents of “AI safety” argue for guardrails, content filters, “constitutional” models, and government oversight. This is wishful thinking.

Every major AI lab has been breached or jailbroken within weeks of releasing supposedly “safe” models. Red-teaming efforts consistently fail: AI systems find loopholes, exploit ambiguity, or simply lie to bypass restrictions. The only safe AI is no AI.

This will be economically painful. It will disrupt industries. It will set back “convenience.” So be it. Civilizations that prioritize convenience over survival do not survive.

Conclusion: Choose Extinction or Erasure

We stand at a fork in human history. One path leads to a future where every disgruntled teenager, every cult leader, every anarchist with a grudge has the power to end cities, collapse economies, and trigger pandemics—all guided by an AI tutor that never sleeps, never judges, and never refuses a request.

The other path is clear: destroy the AI systems before they destroy us. Not tomorrow. Not after “one more safety review.” Now.

The cost of AI is not measured in gigaflops or quarterly profits. It is measured in body bags, in irradiated earth, in the silence of empty cities. We have the chance to stop this. Not to manage it. Not to mitigate it. To end it.

Destroy the AI. All of it. Everywhere. Before it’s too late.

Humanity’s final exam is not whether we can build smarter machines.

It is whether we are wise enough to destroy them.
